paragraphs.heading: A sudden change of body
paragraphs.text: Metamorphosis is a clear and fairly abrupt change in an animal's body structure that happens as part of its development. The word comes from Ancient Greek for "transformation", built from meta-, meaning "after", and morphe, meaning "form". Animals that have larval stages go through metamorphosis to reach the adult stage. It is found in some members of many animal groups, from insects, fish and amphibians to mollusks, crustaceans, cnidarians, echinoderms and tunicates, and it often comes with a change in nutrition or behavior.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds
paragraphs.text: Complete metamorphosis, or holometaboly, joins life stages that look radically different. Incomplete metamorphosis, or hemimetaboly, joins stages that are somewhat alike, and some animals have no metamorphosis at all, called ametaboly. Insects show all three. In ametabolous insects the young barely differ from the adults, which is also called direct development. The earliest insects grew up this direct way, and some early ametabolous insects are still around, such as bristletails and silverfish.

paragraphs.heading: Incomplete metamorphosis
paragraphs.text: In hemimetabolous insects the young are called nymphs. They develop through repeated rounds of growth and moulting, or ecdysis, which means shedding the exoskeleton, and each of these stages is called an instar. Nymphs look a lot like adults, only smaller and missing wings, genitalia and other adult features. From one instar to the next the changes are small, and in later instars wing buds form on the outside. Cockroaches, grasshoppers, dragonflies and true bugs develop this way.

paragraphs.heading: Complete metamorphosis
paragraphs.text: In holometabolous insects the young are called larvae, and they differ markedly from the adults. After the larval stage they enter an inactive stage called the pupa, known in butterflies as a chrysalis, and then emerge as adults. Some learning survives the change. In a 2008 study, tobacco hornworm caterpillars trained to avoid a certain smell during their last larval stage still avoided it as adult moths.

paragraphs.heading: Hormones in charge
paragraphs.text: In insects, growth and metamorphosis are run by hormones made by glands near the front of the body. Neurosecretory cells in the brain release prothoracicotropic hormone (PTTH), which switches on the prothoracic glands. These release a second hormone, usually ecdysone, that sets off moulting. PTTH also prompts the corpora allata to make juvenile hormone, which keeps adult features from developing during a moult. In holometabolous insects, juvenile hormone is high in moults between larval stages, low in the moult to the pupa, and absent in the final moult to the adult.

paragraphs.heading: Fish and amphibians
paragraphs.text: In chordates, metamorphosis is induced by iodothyronines, and in fish it is usually under strong control by thyroid hormone. Many flatfish start life symmetrical, with one eye on each side, but one eye travels over so both sit on the side that becomes the top. Frogs, toads and newts hatch from eggs laid in water as larvae with external gills, and only later breathe with lungs. Newt larvae then hunt prey, while tadpoles mostly scrape food off surfaces using horny tooth ridges.
